William Shakespeare. An English playwright and poet whose thirty-nine plays and one hundred fifty-four sonnets are widely considered the greatest achievement in English literature and perhaps in all literature. Born in fifteen sixty-four in the market town of Stratford-upon-Avon, he moved to London in his late twenties and became the preeminent dramatist of the Elizabethan and Jacobean eras, shaping the template for tragedy, comedy, and history plays that has never been surpassed. His fusion of linguistic exuberance, psychological penetration, and moral ambiguity created characters and scenes that have resonated for four centuries.

Shakespeare was born to John Shakespeare, a glovemaker, and Mary Arden. He was educated in Latin and rhetoric at the local grammar school but did not attend university. He married Anne Hathaway at eighteen—she was already pregnant with their daughter. He left Stratford for London in the late fifteen eighties, leaving family behind. He became an actor and playwright in the newly robust London theatre scene. By fifteen ninety-two he was established enough that rival playwrights were envious of his success.

Shakespeare joined the Lord Chamberlain's Men, later the King's Men after James the First's accession. He was a shareholder in the Globe Theatre, built in fifteen ninety-nine, where most of his plays premiered. He wrote continuously for three decades. Early comedies and history plays came in the fifteen nineties. Great tragedies followed from sixteen hundred to sixteen eight. Final romances came from sixteen nine to sixteen thirteen. He returned to Stratford around sixteen thirteen and died at fifty-two.

His canonical tragedies remain supreme. Hamlet, written around sixteen hundred, tells of the Danish prince who feigns madness while avenging his father's murder. Indecision and introspection are the action. It contains more famous lines and speeches than any other play. Macbeth, written around sixteen six, depicts a Scottish general who murders the king after witches' prophecies. His guilt-driven descent into paranoia and tyranny follows. It is the shortest tragedy, often called the most intense.

Othello, written around sixteen three or sixteen four, depicts a Moorish general driven to murder his innocent wife by the manipulations of Iago. Racism, jealousy, and manipulation become psychological engines. King Lear, written around sixteen five or sixteen six, shows an aging king who divides his kingdom among his daughters based on flattery, loses power, and descends into madness on the heath. It is often cited as the greatest tragedy. Romeo and Juliet, written around fifteen ninety-five, presents young lovers from feuding families. They fall in love and die. It is the definitive love tragedy, though written relatively early in his career.

His comedies and romances are equally significant. A Midsummer Night's Dream, written around fifteen ninety-five or fifteen ninety-six, features lovers and fairies in an enchanted forest. Romance, magic, and comic confusion resolve by dawn. The Merchant of Venice, written around fifteen ninety-six or fifteen ninety-seven, shows Portia, an heiress bound by her father's will to marry the suitor who chooses the correct casket. Shylock, a Jewish moneylender, demands a pound of flesh from the merchant Antonio. The Tempest, written around sixteen ten or sixteen eleven, features the sorcerer Prospero, rightful Duke of Milan, using magic to shipwreck his brother on an island to restore his daughter Miranda. It is often read as Shakespeare's farewell to theatre.

Shakespeare's innovations in form and language were revolutionary. Iambic pentameter—unrhymed lines of ten syllables, five iambs—provides the backbone of dramatic verse. This gives speech a natural rhythm while allowing flexibility for rhetorical emphasis and emotional variation. He used soliloquy as introspection. Characters address the audience directly, revealing inner conflict and psychological nuance. Hamlet's "To be or not to be," Macbeth's descent into nihilism, Iago's motiveless malignity—all are dramatized through soliloquy.

His linguistic abundance is evident everywhere. Puns, wordplay, neologisms, and metaphorical denseness characterize his language. Shakespeare expanded English vocabulary dramatically, coining or first recording hundreds of words. His psychological realism was revolutionary. Characters act from mixed motives, evolve through the play, contradict themselves. They are not stock figures but complex, self-aware beings with desires, doubts, and rationalizations. His structural flexibility blends verse and prose, serious and comic scenes, main plot and subplots, giving the impression of life rather than mechanical design.

Shakespeare is the supreme literary genius of English culture and arguably of world civilization. His plays became the text of English education and cultural transmission. Every educated English speaker knows passages, allusions, and plot summaries. His influence is total. He defined what theatre could be—psychological depth, philosophical reach, linguistic exuberance. His template of tragedy and comedy has been the measure ever since. The Romantic poets elevated him to quasi-religious status. The Victorians made him the apex of literature itself. The twentieth century deconstructed him but never escaped him. Modernists grappled with his authority. Post-colonialists reckoned with The Tempest and The Merchant of Venice. Feminist critics reclaimed female characters. The plays continued to be performed and reinterpreted in every era. He stands with Homer and Dante as a writer whose work has shaped the possibilities of literature itself.
